cultivar: Taiwan native mountain tea (Camellia formosensis), including the TTES #24 selection
processing: Leaf from wild, semi-wild or planted native trees, hand-picked and usually made as an orthodox black (withered, rolled, fully oxidised, dried); some producers make a rolled oolong or a green, and a few press the black into cakes.
harvest_season: Spring (March–May) is the main harvest from the mountain trees, with a smaller summer picking; harvesting on national forest land is restricted.
appearance_dry: Long, uneven, twisted dark strips with some larger leaves and stems, visibly less uniform than cultivated tea.
appearance_wet: Uneven, slightly leathery leaves in brown and copper, of different sizes.
taste_profile: A cooling menthol-and-woody note with herbal, slightly medicinal depth, dark honey and a long, dry-sweet finish; less malty and wilder than Assam-type black.

brewing.notes: Around 90 °C with short gongfu steeps or three minutes Western-style; the aromatic edge shows best when it is not pushed.

vintage_note: Sold by harvest year, by area and increasingly by cultivar (TTES #24), in small quantities at prices that vary wildly. Treat 'wild' on the label as a claim, since genuinely wild-harvested tea is scarce and much comes from planted native-tea seedlings. Black lots keep two or three years and a few producers age pressed cakes.
description:
Taiwan shan cha, 'mountain tea', is the island's native tea plant, now treated as its own species, Camellia formosensis, which grows wild in the central, southern and eastern mountains of the island, with a distinct population in Taitung. It is the wild parent of Ruby 18, which is where that tea's mint-and-cinnamon note comes from, and in the last decade or so it has become a small speciality in its own right, mostly as black tea.

The trees are tall and uneven, picked by hand from wild or semi-wild stands and, increasingly, from planted seedlings, because harvesting on national forest land is restricted. Most producers make an orthodox black, withered, rolled, fully oxidised and dried, which suits the leaf's character; some make a rolled oolong or a green, and a few press the black tea into cakes. The Tea Research and Extension Station has also bred cultivar number 24 from the Yongkang population, so cultivated shan cha is beginning to appear with a cultivar name.

The cup is unlike any other black tea: a cooling menthol-and-woody note, herbal and slightly medicinal depth, dark honey and a long, dry-sweet finish, with less malt and more wildness than Assam-type tea. Brew it at around 90 degrees with short gongfu steeps or three minutes Western-style; it is not harsh, but the aromatic edge comes through best when it is not pushed.

It is sold by harvest year, by area, and increasingly by cultivar, in small quantities at prices that vary wildly. Treat 'wild' on the label as a claim: genuinely wild-harvested tea is scarce, and much of what is sold comes from planted native-tea seedlings, which is fine as long as it is said. Spring leaf is the main harvest, with a smaller summer picking.

Drink it next to Ruby 18 to taste where the famous 'Taiwan fragrance' came from.
sources_note: Botanical status (Camellia sinensis f. formosensis, sometimes treated as Camellia formosensis) and the 2019 release of TTES #24 Shan Yun from Yongkang material are from memory; the list of wild populations is approximate. Category set to black because that is how most of it is sold.
history:
Taiwan's native tea plant grows in the low and middle mountains of the centre, south and east of the island, and local strains differ in flavour. Han settlers were already going into the Shuishalian area to pick and make it before 1697, and the result was called Shuishalian tea.

For much of the twentieth century botanists filed it under Camellia sinensis or the Assam variety. DNA work in 2009 led to its treatment as a separate species, Camellia formosensis, with the Taitung population named as the variety yungkangensis, Yongkang mountain tea.

Breeders at Yuchi crossed it with Burmese large-leaf Assam to create Ruby 18, and cultivar number 24 was later bred from the Yongkang population alone.
